$comment: THE CROSS-REPO CONTRACT. Every invariant that spans capucor-web, capucor-os and
capucor-docs, in one machine-readable place instead of prose in two AGENTS.md files.
WHY IT EXISTS. The 2026-08-04 audit kept finding the same four classes of drift —
coupled dependencies, the provisioning/schema contract, backup coverage, and files
duplicated on purpose — and every single one was caught by a person noticing, not by
anything failing. Drift that only a careful reader catches is drift that ships.
HOW IT IS ENFORCED. `capucor-os/scripts/audit-cross-repo.mjs` (npm run audit) reads
this file and checks every class against all three repos. It is READ-ONLY: it changes
nothing, writes nothing, and touches no production state.
WHY THREE COPIES. capucor-docs holds the canonical copy; capucor-web and capucor-os
each carry a byte-identical vendored copy under contracts/. A CI job runs in ONE
repo's checkout and cannot see its siblings, so a vendored copy is the only way the
in-repo test (src/__tests__/cross-repo-contract.test.ts) can enforce anything from
here. The cross-repo audit compares the three copies to each other, so a drifted copy
is caught by the same command it belongs to. Edit the capucor-docs copy first.

coupledDependencies.why: Next, OpenNext and Wrangler are a runtime TRIPLE, not three independent packages: OpenNext 1.20.x requires Next >=16.2.11, and moving one side alone can make a clean install select an adapter whose Next peer range the app does not satisfy. React and supabase-js are shared because both Workers render the same components and speak to the same PostgREST. All are pinned EXACT (no caret) on purpose — PH-01 pinned them after an unverified runtime pair shipped.

node.why: The dev box runs Node 24 / npm 11. CI ran Node 20 until 2026-08-03 and a lockfile written by npm 11 was rejected outright by npm 10. `.nvmrc` and the `setup-node` step in ci.yml must move together or that trap returns.

provisioning.why: A client signs on capucor.com and capucor-web starts a write whose schema lives in capucor-os. A rename on either side produces NO compile error and NO failing test in either repo. The symptom is a paying client whose durable portal stage keeps retrying.
provisioning.blindSpot: Since migration 017 an `after insert` trigger (client_orgs_default_entity -> ensure_default_entity) runs INSIDE the provisioning insert. If it ever raises, the insert aborts and a paying client gets no portal access. The two UNIT tripwires cannot see this and never will — one drives an in-memory fake, the other reads table invariants out of the migration text; both stay green against a trigger that raises on every insert. That is a permanent property of what they are, not a gap to close.
provisioning.blindSpotCleared: CLEARED — and it is covered continuously, so this is not outstanding work. (1) PO-01 proved it live on 2026-08-03: a throwaway org inserted into production `client_orgs` over PostgREST with the exact column shape provisionFromSignedProposal uses, one `is_primary` entity created, all eight name/reg/tax fields copied, cascade clean on delete — 22 checks, 0 failures. (2) Migration 018 then altered the function (`set search_path = ''`), which by PO-01's own rule required re-proving. (3) `capucor-os/e2e/global-setup.ts` re-proves it on EVERY run of `npm run e2e`: it inserts a real fixture org and THROWS BY NAME ('migration 017's ensure_default_entity trigger did not fire') if the default entity is not there. It ran green on 2026-08-05, after 018. That is why it is listed as a third tripwire above.
provisioning.blindSpotWatchOut: The e2e suite is deliberately NOT in CI (npm ci + a browser download on every push), so this coverage is real but on-demand. Re-run `npm run e2e` after any change to `entities`, to `ensure_default_entity()`, or to the trigger — that is now the live seam test, replacing the hand-run SQL in PO-01's Verify section.

handSynced.why: These files exist in both app repos and a one-sided edit costs money or breaks a seam, with no compile error and no failing test. The per-repo digests below are what lets a SINGLE repo's CI notice a one-sided edit: change the file, the digest moves, that repo goes red naming its counterpart. Regenerate the values with `npm run audit -- --print-digests` in capucor-os and paste them into all three copies of this file.

pairModes.byte: The two copies must be identical after whitespace normalisation.
pairModes.code: The two copies must be identical after comments and blank lines are stripped. Each repo keeps its own explanatory banner — they all carry one, and they should.
pairModes.independent: The two copies legitimately differ. No cross-repo equality is asserted; the digests still pin each side so a one-sided edit is visible. `expectedCodeDiffLines` bounds how far apart they are allowed to drift.

files.why: Both repos price the same proposals off the same `brackets` table — capucor.com when a lead builds one, capucor.app when staff amend one. Drift means two different quotes for one selection.

Both repos price the same proposals off the same `brackets` table. It carried three sanctioned divergent lines until 2026-08-06 — capucor-os logged the bracket-fetch failure through `lib/log.ts`, capucor-web through console.error — and giving capucor-web the same `lib/log.ts` collapsed that to zero. A BOUNDED divergence still needs a reader to judge whether the bound is measuring the right thing; an equality does not.

PRICING_ADDONS is the server-side WHITELIST of accepted add-on slugs and their prices, not display strings. Reprice an add-on in one repo only and the two apps quote different totals, or one silently drops an add-on the other charges for.

Both repos mint into the SAME unique client_orgs.slug column from two different Workers. A divergence in the slugify rule or the collision suffix surfaces as a unique-constraint violation on a paying client's first insert.

The retry runner in capucor-os rebuilds a capucor-web message from this file and sends it under the ORIGINAL idempotency key. A divergence means the retry sends different content from the original, inside Resend's 24-hour idempotency window.

knownDuplicates.why: Same-path files that are identical in both repos but are not worth the friction of a pinned digest — design primitives, thin client factories, and generated types. The audit still enforces the declared relationship across repos. Its real job is the INVERSE check: an identical same-path file that appears in neither this list nor handSynced is reported, so a new accidental duplicate has to be classified rather than quietly accumulate.

entries.why: shadcn/Base-Nova primitives. Drift is a visual inconsistency between the marketing site and the OS, not a data bug — but the two surfaces are meant to look like one product.
The service-role and cookieless client factories. Both repos read the same tables under the same policies; a divergence here is a silent-zero-rows bug.
One-time link tokens minted by capucor-web and consumed by flows both repos touch.
cn() plus firstOfNextMonth(), which decides the first debit date shown on a proposal and written into a subscription period.
The per-IP token bucket. Namespacing rules differ per repo but the bucket implementation must not.
On Cloudflare the real client IP is CF-Connecting-IP; x-forwarded-for is the worker loopback and collapses every visitor into one bucket. Both repos rate-limit and both record signer IPs.

Structured one-line-JSON logging into Workers Logs. `evt` is treated as an API — a saved Cloudflare query built on one repo's event name should mean the same thing in the other. It sits here rather than in handSynced deliberately: a one-sided edit is a log line in the wrong shape, not a wrong price or a broken seam, and PH-10 kept digests to the five files where a one-sided edit costs money. Cross-repo equality is still enforced.

The scheduled-workflow watchdog, byte-identical in both repos because each copy selects its own crons from scheduledWorkflows by GITHUB_REPOSITORY. A one-sided edit means one repo's crons stop being watched — caught here, cross-repo, with no digest to re-record every time the script is touched.

The deploy-drift check (R-12a), byte-identical in both repos because each copy checks its own repo, selected from deployDrift.deployments by GITHUB_REPOSITORY. A one-sided edit means one surface stops being watched for shipping behind master — caught here, cross-repo, with no digest to re-record every time the script is touched.
The PH-08b body cap. Per-route limits differ; the content-length-then-running-count helper must not.
The HMAC that gates detailed /api/health. Both CI workflows sign with the same scheme; a divergence silently drops one repo back to the public view.
Generated from ONE Supabase project by `npm run db:types`. If the two copies differ, one repo regenerated after a migration and the other did not — which is the only way this file can drift at all.

Toolchain configuration. Both Workers are built by the same pinned Next/OpenNext pair, so a divergence here means one repo is being linted, styled or bundled differently from the thing it is supposed to be identical to.

The same incremental-cache override in both, but the COMMENTS deliberately differ: capucor-web's describes real ISR on / and /pricing, while capucor-os's records that the same comment was copied over in Phase 1a and was false there — no /api/revalidate, and `revalidate` is banned on every per-user route. Each Worker must keep its OWN KV namespace regardless; both apps have a "/" route key, so a shared one makes one app serve the other's cached page.
Shared URLs and senders, but each repo declares its own origin defaults.
Phase 3 dropped the OS-only types (SubscriptionSummary, SubscriptionStatus, ProposalRow) from capucor-web's copy. Only the pricing shapes are shared — this is no longer a straight mirror.

syncedTriples.why: Files that must be identical in all three repos. Checked repo-to-repo by the cross-repo audit only; a digest recorded inside a file cannot cover that file itself.

routeSeam.why: One Worker per domain, split by host-based redirects, with each repo holding one half of the table. A path dropped from the wrong list turns an old bookmark or an already-sent email link into a 404.

os.note: /proposal/:path* is the one that looks removable and is not: the signing document lives on capucor.com, but proposal links in already-sent emails were minted against capucor.app.

routeSeam.forbiddenWhy: A 301 on a POST downgrades it to GET and drops the body. Redirecting /_next or /brand off capucor.app strips the CSS and logo from every portal page — which is why the lists are explicit rather than a negative-lookahead catch-all.

backup.why: The dump is the only copy of the signed debit-order mandates. Supabase Free includes no platform backups and no PITR.
keyPrefixDeclaredIn: Cloudflare R2 lifecycle rule — 185-day expiry (dashboard only, NOT checkable from here)
Cloudflare R2 bucket-lock rule — 180-day retention (dashboard only, NOT checkable from here)
backup.keyPrefixWarning: One fact in three places and only the code half is testable. Changing KEY_PREFIX without changing both Cloudflare rules silently un-retains and un-expires every object.
backup.zeroDependencyWhy: These jobs are checkout + setup-node + `node script.mjs` BY DESIGN. No `npm ci`, which is the difference between a run billing one minute against the free 2,000 and billing five. Do not add one.
backup.weakestLink: The dump exists only if cron-backup.yml keeps running, and a workflow that stops running produces an empty Actions history nobody looks at. That is now watched — see `scheduledWorkflows` below. What remains unwatchable from inside these repos is the quiet period itself: the watchdog runs on push, so it reports the silence on the first push back rather than during it.
backup.localDumpLocation: capucor-os/scripts/backup-dir.mjs, overridable with CAPUCOR_BACKUP_DIR (unset in CI, which keeps the in-repo default).
backup.localDumpLocationWhy: FOUND AND FIXED 2026-08-06. The dev box's checkout is at C:\Users\zjak\OneDrive\Documents\..., so the gitignored `backups/` directory was syncing every local dump to OneDrive — seven of them, each holding the 32 signed debit-order mandates with signature images, signer IPs, SARS numbers and POPIA consent records. Not a breach (Zjak's own Microsoft account) but an unstated third-party processing location that no document mentioned and that the R2 retention story said nothing about. ⚠️ THE TRANSFERABLE LESSON: gitignoring a directory keeps it out of git and does NOTHING about a sync client, and every document here said 'gitignored, keep it off GitHub' as though those were the same statement. Zjak's decision 2026-08-06: move the directory outside the synced tree, keep all seven dumps. CAPUCOR_BACKUP_DIR now points at C:/Users/zjak/capucor-backups. ⚠️ RESIDUAL: OneDrive keeps deleted files in its cloud recycle bin for roughly 30 days, so the synced copies persist there until they age out or are purged by hand.
backup.localDumpsAreNotARetentionTier: Local dumps are a convenience for taking a snapshot before a risky migration. They are NOT one of the two backup destinations — those are the GitHub Actions artifact and the R2 object, both produced by cron-backup.yml on a runner, neither of which reads this directory. Deleting every local dump loses nothing that matters.

scheduledWorkflows.why: Everything irreplaceable here is kept alive by a GitHub Actions cron: the daily database dump (both destinations), the email/fulfilment reconciler, and the POPIA lead prune. They all fail the same way — they stop, and nothing says so. `scripts/schedule-watchdog.mjs` asks the Actions API when each one last SUCCEEDED and fails the build when the answer is older than `maxAgeDays`.
scheduledWorkflows.watchesForSilenceNotCause: The check is deliberately cause-agnostic. Asking 'is the workflow disabled?' covers one failure mode; asking 'when did it last succeed?' covers that one plus an expired secret, an exhausted Actions allowance, a renamed file, a deleted schedule and a job that has been failing every night. A watchdog written against a named cause stops working the moment the cause is different.
scheduledWorkflows.inactivityRule: MEASURED 2026-08-06, and it corrects a claim that was carried in three places. GitHub's documentation scopes the auto-disable to public repositories: 'In a public repository, scheduled workflows are automatically disabled when no repository activity has occurred in 60 days.' capucor-webpage IS public (unauthenticated api.github.com read → 200), so its two crons are exposed to exactly that rule. capucor-os is PRIVATE (→ 404) and holds cron-backup.yml, so the 60-day rule as documented does not reach the backup at all. The private repo's analogous silent-stop risk is different — it bills against a finite free Actions allowance that a public repo does not have. Neither repo is safe by being the other kind, which is why the watchdog checks recency rather than visibility.
scheduledWorkflows.cannotFireDuringQuiet: The watchdog runs on push. It cannot fire during the quiet period that causes the disable, and no in-repo mechanism can — every in-repo mechanism is hosted by the thing that goes quiet. Stated rather than papered over, with the one external control, in capucor-docs/operations/backup-watchdog.md.
scheduledWorkflows.watchdogWhy: Both copies are byte-identical and each watches only its OWN repo's crons, selected by matching GITHUB_REPOSITORY against githubRepos. A CI job cannot read a sibling repo's Actions API with its own GITHUB_TOKEN, so one watchdog covering both repos would need a cross-repo PAT — a long-lived credential to avoid duplicating a 250-line file. Two copies, no credential.

workflows.why: This is the ONLY backup of the signed debit-order mandates — Supabase Free has no platform backups and no PITR. If it has stopped, both destinations have stopped with it.

Drains durable email and signed-proposal fulfilment retries. If it has stopped, a paying client's portal stage retries forever and no email is ever resent. Five days rather than three because it is weekday-only: a long weekend plus a public holiday is a legitimate gap of nearly four.
The POPIA retention job. If it has stopped, personal data is being kept past the retention policy — a compliance failure whose only symptom is nothing happening.
Flips proposals past expires_at to expired. If it has stopped, an expired quote stays signable at a price that is no longer offered.

scheduledWorkflows.maxAgeWhy: Three days for a daily job, not one. GitHub delays scheduled runs under load — measured on capucor-webpage 2026-08-06, jobs scheduled for 03:15/03:30 UTC actually ran between 06:01 and 06:44 — and a run can be skipped outright. A threshold that goes red on one late night is a threshold somebody switches off.
scheduledWorkflows.reportsFailureDoesNotFailOnIt: A failing LATEST run is reported as context but is not itself a failure here. GitHub already emails on a failed scheduled run, so a red night is loud without us; silence is what nothing else covers, and a job that keeps failing crosses the staleness threshold on its own. Failing on it would also leave every push red after an intentional R2 fire drill until the next nightly run.
scheduledWorkflows.drill: SCHEDULE_WATCHDOG_DRILL=stale forces maxAgeDays to 0 so a healthy cron reads as overdue; =disabled rewrites the reported state to disabled_inactivity. Both are workflow_dispatch inputs on watchdog.yml, touch no secret and mutate nothing. Same reasoning as R2_FIRE_DRILL: an unexercised failure path is not a control.

deployDrift.why: R-12. Nothing watched capucor-os `master` drifting ahead of what is actually deployed, and on 2026-08-24 it drifted by two merges before being closed by hand. ADR 0010 part 1 made this the NORMAL state rather than an exception: deployment is now a manual dispatch on both surfaces, so a merged fix is no longer a shipped fix and drift no longer self-corrects. `scripts/deploy-drift.mjs` asks the Actions API for the newest SUCCESSFUL run of each repo's deploy workflow, takes its `head_sha`, and compares that commit to the tip of the release branch.
deployDrift.measuredEvidence: MEASURED 2026-08-24, and it is why this exists rather than being proposed. capucor-webpage's last successful production deploy was `f99bc85` at 14:20Z on 2026-08-20 — the ADR 0010 verification dispatch. `master` was `3896e1c`, `ahead_by` 21, including the Node 24 Actions upgrade and four `db.ts` regenerations. Four days, twenty-one commits, no signal anywhere. The gap this check closes was open and occupied at the moment the check was written.
deployDrift.questionIsComparisonNotAge: ⚠️ THE OBVIOUS SHAPE IS WRONG. The cron watchdog beside this asks 'when did the workflow last succeed?' and that question does not transfer. A deploy is not scheduled and has no cadence it is supposed to keep, so an age threshold on the WORKFLOW silently invents a release cadence ADR 0010 deliberately declined to set — and it is reset by a deploy that happened for an unrelated reason while the drift that matters persists. The question here is a COMPARISON: is the deployed commit still the tip of the branch, and if not, how long has the oldest unshipped commit been sitting there.
deployDrift.measuresOldestUnshippedCommitNotCommitCo: The gate is the AGE OF THE OLDEST UNSHIPPED COMMIT, never `ahead_by`. Commit count is noise: twenty-one commits of generated types is not riskier than one broken route, and gating on it would go red on a busy afternoon and green on a fortnight of neglect. Age measures the thing that actually went wrong — how long a merged fix has not been a shipped fix. `ahead_by` is reported as context and must not become a threshold.
deployDrift.equalityWouldBeSwitchedOff: ⚠️ AND IT MUST NOT BE AN EQUALITY CHECK. Under ADR 0010 `master` ahead of production is the normal state, so a check that fails whenever the deployed SHA is not the tip goes red on every single merge. The contract already learned this one for the crons — see `scheduledWorkflows.maxAgeWhy` — and the lesson is the same: a threshold that cries wolf is a threshold somebody switches off, which is how a control becomes a comment.
deployDrift.githubReposWhy: The owner/name slugs are NOT repeated here. They are already canonical in `scheduledWorkflows.githubRepos`, and a second copy is a second thing to forget when a repo is renamed. `scripts/deploy-drift.mjs` resolves this pointer rather than carrying its own map.
deployDrift.hostedByTheWatchdogWorkflow: It is a second STEP in watchdog.yml, not a second workflow. Same trigger (push), same reason (a push is the one moment we know a human is present), same zero-dependency rule, and the permissions it needs are already granted there: `actions: read` for the run, `contents: read` for the compare. No new workflow, no new credential, no new infrastructure and no additional Actions minutes — two extra API calls in a job that already runs.
deployDrift.bothCopiesIdentical: Both copies are byte-identical and each checks only its OWN repo, selected by matching GITHUB_REPOSITORY against githubRepos — exactly as the cron watchdog does, and for the same reason: a CI job cannot read a sibling repo's Actions API with its own GITHUB_TOKEN, so one copy covering both repos would need a long-lived cross-repo PAT. Two copies, no credential. Enforced by the `scripts/deploy-drift.mjs` entry in knownDuplicates.

deployments.why: capucor.app — the client portal and internal command centre. Unshipped commits here are unshipped fixes to a surface real clients sign in to, and since ADR 0003 split validation from deployment nothing ships without a human dispatching it.

capucor.com — the marketing funnel that mints proposals. This is the repo the 2026-08-24 measurement found four days and twenty-one commits adrift, and the repo whose deploy.yml has been dispatched exactly once since ADR 0010 part 1 created it.

deployDrift.maxAgeWhy: Seven days, and the number is a judgement rather than a measurement. capucor-webpage's four-day drift on 2026-08-24 was deliberate — deploy.yml was awaiting an intentional deployment — and going red on it would have been noise. The capucor.com incident of 2026-08-06 ran to two weeks and was plainly not fine. Seven splits them and turns a merged-but-unshipped fix red inside one working week. ⚠️ It is deliberately LOOSE: set tight enough to force a deploy schedule this stops being a hygiene check and becomes a release cadence, which is an amendment to ADR 0010 and belongs there rather than here.
deployDrift.cannotSeeProduction: ⚠️ IT DOES NOT OBSERVE PRODUCTION, and the distinction matters. A green deploy run proves `wrangler` uploaded a build; it does not prove the Worker is serving that code. A rollback in the Cloudflare dashboard, a hand-run `npx wrangler deploy` from a laptop, or a deploy that succeeded against the wrong account are all invisible from the Actions API. True ground truth would need the deployed app to advertise its build SHA and this job to fetch it — but the detailed /api/health response is HMAC-signed with SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY, and putting a production secret into a job that runs on EVERY push is a worse trade than the gap it closes. Stated rather than papered over.
deployDrift.cannotFireDuringQuiet: Same limit as the cron watchdog, and sharper here, because a push is the very thing that CREATES drift. A repo that goes quiet while drifted stays silent until someone pushes again. The 2026-08-24 measurement is the worked example: capucor-webpage's drift began on 2026-08-20 and would have been reported on the next push, four days later — loudly, and four days before anyone found it by hand.
deployDrift.cannotJudgeWhetherDriftMatters: Twenty-one commits of generated types and one broken route look identical from here. This check reports that production is not the tip and how long that has been true; deciding whether it matters is a human reading the commit list.
deployDrift.doesNotCloseCiSilence: ⚠️ IT CLOSES HALF OF R-12. The risk records two gaps: deploy drift, and CI SILENCE — the 2026-08-06 incident in which GitHub dropped push triggers on capucor-webpage so ci.yml never ran at all. This check does not detect that, and the detector is self-referential: if push triggers are being dropped, the watchdog hosting this step is not running either. R-12 should be split rather than closed — R-12a is this; R-12b is CI silence and remains open.
deployDrift.drill: DEPLOY_DRIFT_DRILL=drift rewrites the observed comparison to 99 commits ahead with an oldest unshipped commit 99 days old, so the common failure and its message are exercised against the REAL API; =never rewrites the observed run to absent, exercising the 'this repo has never deployed' path. Both are workflow_dispatch inputs on watchdog.yml, touch no secret and mutate nothing. Same reasoning as SCHEDULE_WATCHDOG_DRILL and R2_FIRE_DRILL: an unexercised failure path is not a control. The drill forces the CONDITION true rather than moving the threshold, because with the deployed SHA at the tip there is no unshipped commit for a threshold of zero to act on.

migrationLedger.evidence: Until 2026-08-06 the ledger SCHEMA did not exist — `select count(*) from information_schema.schemata where schema_name = 'supabase_migrations'` returned 0, measured read-only on 2026-08-05 and again immediately before the repair. The repair created it with `supabase migration repair --status applied` (the CLI's own command, so the DDL is the CLI's and not hand-rolled) and backfilled the 21 CLI-parseable versions 001-008 and 010-022. `supabase db push --dry-run` now reports `Remote database is up to date`. The schema was proven unmoved either side: `npm run db:check` passed 27 tables from 23 migrations, and `npm run db:types` regenerated with NO diff against the committed src/types/db.ts.
migrationLedger.pushAllowedWhy: Reviewed and approved by Zjak on 2026-08-06, then executed against a proven backup. The ban existed because a 2026-08-04 dry run proposed replaying every plain `create table` migration from 001 against a live database that already had all 27 tables. With the ledger honest, the dry run proposes nothing. `npm run db:check` remains the gate that actually proves the result and still runs in CI — db push replaces the apply step, not the proof. NOTE: the original approval also cited 'db diff becomes usable' as a benefit. That turned out to be FALSE on this machine — see driftDetection. The audit trail and the honest ledger are the real payoff; the drift half was solved a different way.
migrationLedger.driftDetection: MEASURED 2026-08-06. `supabase db diff` — the tool for catching a change made out of band in the Supabase dashboard — is NOT reachable from the dev box. It needs a shadow database, which needs Docker, which is not installed; the command dies at 'Creating shadow database'. Three options were weighed: install Docker Desktop locally (heavy, licensing question, and only runs when someone remembers), run `db diff` in CI (a runner has Docker, but `--linked` needs the production DATABASE PASSWORD as a repo secret — a credential neither repo holds and strictly more powerful than the service-role key), or take the affordable subset. Zjak chose the subset. `scripts/check-schema-drift.mjs` now checks BOTH directions using the PostgREST OpenAPI document it was already fetching: migrations ⊆ live (the original gate) and live ⊆ migrations (undeclared objects). Zero new credentials, zero new infrastructure, runs in the CI gate that already exists. Proven clean against production on 2026-08-06 and drilled by removing migration 017 locally — it reported all seven register tables as undeclared and exited 1.
migrationLedger.driftDetectionLimits: The reverse direction sees TABLES AND COLUMNS ONLY. Triggers, functions, RLS policies and constraints stay invisible — the same blind spot `db:check` always had, now stated rather than implied. A dashboard-added trigger or a loosened policy is still uncatchable from here. ⛔ Do not describe the reverse check as a replacement for `db diff`; it is the part of `db diff` that a machine without Docker can afford. If that residual ever needs closing, the honest options are the two that were declined above, and the CI one costs a production database password.
migrationLedger.ledgerInvariant: Every version in the remote ledger MUST have a matching local migration file. A remote-only version is not harmlessly ignored: `supabase db push` aborts with 'Remote migration versions not found in local migrations directory' and EVERY push stays blocked until the row is removed. MEASURED 2026-08-06 on CLI 2.93.1 — the repair first backfilled 0091/0092 for the two 009 files, and the dry run refused to run at all. This is why the two files below are deliberately absent from the ledger.
migrationLedger.filenamePatternWhy: The Supabase CLI parses a migration version as the leading digits up to the first underscore. A letter-suffixed name is not merely mis-ordered — the file is not treated as a migration at all. The CLI does print `Skipping migration <file>... (file name must match pattern)`, so it is visible if you read the output, but nothing fails.
migrationLedger.knownNonConformingWhy: There were two 009_ files until 2026-08-03. They were suffixed rather than renumbered so the file order still reflects when they were actually applied. They are applied in the database and are deliberately NOT in the ledger: the CLI cannot see the files, so it will never propose them, and recording them by hand blocks every push (see ledgerInvariant). Decided 2026-08-06 — the ledger's two-row hole lives in prose here rather than renaming files that four documents reference. If they are ever renumbered to conforming names, backfill the matching versions in the SAME change.

fixedPaths.why: Two SessionStart hooks in .claude/hooks/ read these files by hard-coded path and grep for a control line. Moving or renaming either breaks the nudge SILENTLY — the hook exits 0 on a missing file by design, so nothing ever reports it.

docs.why: The board, the tracker and the two AGENTS.md files are load-bearing navigation. A relative link that stopped resolving is the cheapest possible drift to catch and the easiest to leave rotting.
docs.linkCheckExcludeWhy: archive/ is frozen history. Its documents cite files at the paths they had when the work was done, and a good number of those files were deleted in Phase 3 of the OS split. Rewriting those links to today's paths would make the record say something that was never true, and deleting them would lose the citation. A link checker that forces a historical document to describe the present is a checker that gets switched off. workspace-root/ is excluded for a different reason: it is a byte-exact VENDORED COPY of the unversioned workspace-root scaffold, and its links are written to resolve from the workspace root where bootstrap.sh deploys it, not from where it is stored. Checked in place, every ./capucor-* link in the vendored AGENTS.md and GEMINI.md resolves one directory too deep and reads as broken — 31 of them when this was added. The DEPLOYED copies at the workspace root ARE checked: root 'AGENTS.md' and 'GEMINI.md' are both linkCheckRoots.
